transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Ben Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (CTO, Apollo), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng), Sofia Perez (Infra)

Summary: quick discovery focused on latency and throughput requirements for Apollo's LLM-powered clinical summarization product. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for p95 latency and sustained throughput (tokens/sec) with streaming responses. Discussed concurrency, batching, KV/prefix cache, and benchmarking plan. Agreed next steps to share pricing and run an initial dedicated pilot benchmark.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency and streaming, token/sec benchmarking, model variants, dedicated capacity configs, security/residency asks

Transcript:
[00:00] Ben Carter: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ben from redwood, i'll kick us off. Maya from our se team is here.
[00:10] Priya Raman: hey thanks ben, appreciate it. quick context — we're building a clinical notes summarization feature, real time-ish, p95 latency needs to be around 400 to 600ms for single-turn summaries, sometimes up to 1s for longer context. throughput wise we need about 60 concurrent active users, avg 200 tokens per request, hoping for sustained about 2k-3k tokens/sec across the service.
[00:35] Maya Singh: cool that helps. when you say p95 400-600ms is that for streamed tokens or final completion?
[00:42] Priya Raman: mostly for streaming initial tokens — UX starts showing first sentence quickly. final completion can be >1s.
[00:48] Liam O'Connor: also important: we send long contexts sometimes 8k tokens, and we use KV cache for patient session context. need caching to avoid reencoding large prefix each time.
[01:05] Ben Carter: got it. sounds like three levers for us: model choice (smaller faster vs higher quality), deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and batching/prefix cache configs. any regulatory constraints?
[01:18] Priya Raman: HIPAA is required, so audit logs, KMS, and VPC/private deployment are on the table. Ideally private deployment but we are open to dedicated if we can get guarantees and data controls.
[01:32] Sofia Perez: from infra side, we need SSO, RBAC, and SIEM integrations, and also need network egress rules for the private option — basically can't have egress to unknown regions.
[01:45] Maya Singh: ok thanks. for the latency targets — 400-600ms p95 for initial streaming — that's tight but doable with the right model and hardware. question: are you measuring p95 per-token or p95 for first-byte? how do you define it today?
[02:00] Priya Raman: our current metric is first-byte p95 for the initial content-bearing token after prompt. we instrument in-app.
[02:08] Ben Carter: good to know. on concurrency: 60 active concurrent users at avg 200 tokens per request equals roughly 12k tokens per second in peak if all active — wait let me do the math. 60 users * 200 tokens = 12,000 tokens total per second per request window if they're all producing tokens in parallel, but many have variable timing — is 2k-3k sustained the more realistic steady-state?
[02:38] Priya Raman: yep that's the sustained number, but we'd like buffer for peaks. around 6k tokens/sec headroom would be ideal.
[02:46] Maya Singh: solid. so for benchmarking we need to emulate streaming behavior and concurrency. our Dedicated offering can reserve GPU pools and give predictable throughput. Hosted can be easiest to start but has burst limits and less isolation; Private gives you full control but requires deployment lead time.
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: any examples of p95 numbers customers hit on dedicated? especially with NVidia H100s or similar?
[03:12] Maya Singh: common reference: on H100-class infra, with quantized Llama-family models, customers see sub-200ms p95 for first tokens on smaller instruction-tuned models at moderate context lengths (2k). Larger contexts and bigger models push that up — 400-600ms p95 is plausible for mid-sized models on dedicated with tuned kernels and KV caching. streaming overhead and network adds few tens of ms.
[03:38] Ben Carter: also note our runtime does continuous batching and will pack requests when it helps throughput — but for tight p95 streaming we can tune batch windows.
[03:47] Priya Raman: what about token/sec benchmarking, how do you measure sustained tokens/sec vs peak?
[03:53] Maya Singh: we usually run two measurements: sustained throughput — long-running worker with steady concurrency to measure tokens/sec and mem pressure; and peak tail benchmarks — sudden burst with ramp and measure p95, p99. We'll want your real prompt set so the token distribution matches.
[04:10] Sofia Perez: how do you handle prefix cache evictions and multi-tenant cache isolation? we can't have patient data cached across tenants.
[04:18] Ben Carter: for Dedicated and Private, cache is per-customer pool and can be configured to never persist to disk. for Hosted we have strict partitioning, TTLs and encryption, but we understand enterprise often asks for Dedicated/Private to remove shared tenancy.
[04:33] Priya Raman: another thing — model rollouts and regressions matter. we need eval hooks so if a new quantized model causes lower QA we can failover.
[04:43] Maya Singh: yep we have rollout policies and quality monitoring integrated in the console. automatic fallback to previous model variant on regressions is supported.
[04:50] Liam O'Connor: for the benchmark can you replicate our network topology? e.g., we run in us-east and some traffic comes from EU — latency differences matter.
[04:59] Maya Singh: we can run regionally in us-east and eu-west to measure cross-region latencies; Dedicated pools can be provisioned in specific regions.
[05:06] Priya Raman: are there any known tradeoffs for streaming vs non-streaming in CPU/GPU utilization?
[05:12] Maya Singh: streaming increases small-packet network overhead and keeps the instance more chatty, also kernel launch patterns differ — but our runtime optimizes for streaming by overlapping decoding and network writes; it can slightly lower raw tokens/sec when compared to batched non-streaming completion for the same hardware, but improves perceived latency.
[05:32] Ben Carter: on instrumentation, we'll share a benchmark harness (JMeter/wrk style + streaming harness) we use — it can replay your prompt set with proper token timing — that'll be part of the benchmark plan.
[05:43] Priya Raman: what's the typical run and data you need from us?
[05:47] Maya Singh: sample prompt set (tokenized), target p95 definitions, representative concurrency profile (burst patterns), and any model preferences. Also a few patient redaction rules to validate latency with pre-processing.
[06:00] Priya Raman: ok we'll aim to send that by Friday.
[06:03] Ben Carter: perfect. quick question about pricing: Dedicated reserved capacity — how granular are configs and what's the expected monthly commitment?
[06:12] Ben Carter: (cont) I can share a pricing worksheet, typical committed units are monthly with options for burst. We'll include example configs for hitting 6k tokens/sec sustained and p95 targets.
[06:24] Sofia Perez: for Private/on-prem, what's the usual deployment time? we can't have lengthy windows for a POC.
[06:29] Maya Singh: Private is heavier — usually 6-8 weeks for full on-prem with compliance checks; for pilots we often do a Dedicated isolated pool in your VPC or our partner cloud which takes 1-2 weeks.
[06:43] Liam O'Connor: curious about kernel assumptions — do you select different kernels for quantized vs fp16 models?
[06:48] Maya Singh: yes, runtime picks kernels and execution paths based on model arch, quantization, and sequence length. quantized paths can be much faster but may have slight quality delta.
[06:58] Priya Raman: do you support dynamic batching policies? we don't want batching to add >100ms to p95.
[07:04] Maya Singh: yes, we configure latency SLOs and batching windows; for sub-second p95s we'll reduce batch windows and rely on prefix cache to keep throughput sane.
[07:12] Ben Carter: can you describe the proposed benchmark steps so we align?
[07:17] Maya Singh: step 1: Apollo provides prompt set and p95 definition. step 2: Redwood configures Dedicated pilot with chosen model(s) in us-east with KV cache settings and autoscaling off for stable baseline. step 3: run sustained throughput test for 1 hour at target concurrency to measure tokens/sec and memory behavior. step 4: run burst/p95 tests with streaming enabled and measure first-byte p95, p99, and tail. step 5: analyze results and tune batching/prefetch/quantization.
[07:48] Priya Raman: that sounds good. what's a typical baseline for 200-token requests at 60 concurrency on a 4-GPU H100 pool?
[07:56] Maya Singh: rough ballpark — depends on model and quantization, but for mid-size instruction-tuned models you might see 3k-10k tokens/sec for a 4xH100 pool with optimized kernels. p95 could be 150-400ms for first byte with streaming on smaller models, 400-800ms for larger. we'll provide concrete numbers in the worksheet.
[08:17] Sofia Perez: any concerns about model caching causing stale results? we need consistent freshness for clinical info.
[08:23] Ben Carter: cache is purely performance-layer; we honor TTLs and can disable caching for sensitive flows. caching doesn't affect model weights.
[08:31] Priya Raman: ok noted. also need SOC2 + HIPAA attestation docs for security review.
[08:36] Ben Carter: we'll attach SOC2 and our HIPAA whitepaper and an architecture note for private deployment.
[08:42] Liam O'Connor: let's talk about success criteria for the pilot — what would you need?
[08:46] Priya Raman: 1) p95 first-byte <=600ms for initial streaming for 90% of cases, 2) sustained tokens/sec >=2k with headroom to 6k, 3) no data leaving VPC for private flows, 4) acceptable quality metrics vs current model.
[09:03] Maya Singh: that's clear. we'll aim the benchmark to validate those.
[09:08] Ben Carter: recap and next steps — Ben to share Dedicated pricing/config and SOC2/HIPAA docs by Friday 9/12; Maya to share benchmark plan and harness and request prompt set by 9/14; Apollo to send tokenized prompts and concurrency profile by 9/13; schedule pilot week of 9/22.
[09:26] Priya Raman: thanks all. quick note: can we get an architecture diagram for the Dedicated pool and how VPC peering/egress is handled?
[09:33] Ben Carter: yes will include architecture diagram in the doc bundle.
[09:37] Sofia Perez: also include expected network flows and ports.
[09:40] Ben Carter: noted.
[09:42] Priya Raman: thanks, that covers it.
[09:44] Ben Carter: awesome, we'll follow up with the docs. bye everyone.

End of transcript.
